hook: A car takes a curve, a planet circles the Sun, a bucket of water whirls overhead without spilling. Each object moves at a steady speed yet is accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. Something has to pull it toward the center. Finding that something, among the real forces, is the whole skill.

ideas: Uniform circular motion: constant speed v = 2πr/T on a circle; the acceleration ac = v²/r points to the center. The period T is the time for one trip; the frequency f = 1/T, in Hz.
The centripetal net force, ΣF toward the center = mv²/r, is supplied by real forces: tension, friction, normal force, gravity, or their parts. Never draw it as an extra arrow.
Speeding up or slowing on a circle adds a tangential acceleration; the total is the vector sum.
Circular orbits: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r) and Kepler's third law, T² = (4π²/GM)r³.

misconception.wrong: An object moving in a circle has a centripetal force pulling it in and a centrifugal force pushing it out, and both go on the free-body diagram.
misconception.right: Only real forces go on the diagram. "Centripetal" names the job of the net force toward the center; there is no outward force. A released object leaves along the tangent, not outward.

summary: Circular motion at constant speed is accelerated motion: a_c = v²/r toward the center, with v = 2πr/T. Real forces (tension, friction, normal force, gravity) must add to a net force mv²/r toward the center; for circular orbits this gives v = √(GM/r) and T² ∝ r³.
